text: Internal parasites impair health in several ways. Chronic nutrient loss: e.g. adult Ascaris feeding in a pig's intestine leaves heavily infested piglets thin and less resistant to infection by 2 months old; in scavenging chickens, various roundworms in the small intestine or gizzard slow growth and reduce condition. Reduced appetite: worms in the stomach/intestine irritate these organs, causing infested animals to eat less — a useful diagnostic clue is that fever plus reduced appetite suggests infectious disease, while reduced appetite with a normal temperature points more toward internal parasites (note: in cattle, stomach parasites are found in the abomasum, the fourth stomach chamber, not the rumen). Diarrhea: from intestinal lining irritation by worms, or from impaired digestion when the liver is damaged, as in Liver Fluke (Fasciola). Coughing: Ascaris larvae migrating through the lungs cause pneumonia and coughing; in cattle, lung worms cause a disease (verminous pneumonia/bronchitis) with signs similar to viral or bacterial disease — mature lung worms live in the bronchi, causing rapid breathing, coughing, and nasal discharge. Rough hair coat: worm burden often combines with poor nutrition, producing symptoms similar to vitamin/mineral deficiency. Anemia: worms can damage the stomach or liver lining and cause bleeding — e.g. red stomach worms (about 1 cm long) in sows suck blood, causing appetite loss and anemia; Fasciola causes bleeding liver lesions and anemia in cattle; as anemia develops, edema (swelling) often appears under the jaw. Reduced immunity: in cattle, the brown stomach worm (Ostertagia, found in the abomasum) actively suppresses immune response. Mortality: Toxocara (a roundworm whose larvae live in the cow) can weaken and sometimes kill calves around 3–4 months old after they ingest larvae through milk in the first 2 weeks of life. Zoonotic risk: Trichinella (a 2–4 mm roundworm forming cysts in pig muscle) causes human illness from undercooked pork, with an initial intestinal phase (abdominal discomfort, diarrhea, nausea within 1–2 days) followed by a muscle phase (aches, itching, fever, chills, joint pain, 2–8 weeks later); Taenia (tapeworm, 2–7 m long, living in humans/dogs, surviving up to 25 years) uses pigs (Taenia Solium) or cattle (Taenia Saginata) as intermediate hosts, causing cysticercosis — people are infected either by eating undercooked pork/beef containing dormant larvae (leading to Taeniasis, often symptom-free besides tiredness and visible tapeworm segments in feces) or by ingesting Taenia eggs from poor hygiene, which can travel to muscle, liver, or brain tissue and eventually cause muscle spasms, dizziness, headaches, or death as old cysts break down.
